summary:
A press release from MyPerfectResume, published via Allwork.Space, announces The Long Shutout report on US long-term unemployment. Analyzing 23 seasonally adjusted monthly Bureau of Labor Statistics data sets (Current Population Survey and JOLTS) covering January 2016 to July 2026, the company finds that 25.9% of unemployed Americans had been out of work at least 27 weeks during the first seven months of 2026, up from 18.9% in 2023. The long-term unemployed population grew 68%, from 1.1 million to 1.9 million, with nearly 2 million in May 2026.

Duration of joblessness is lengthening: median unemployment duration rose from 8.9 weeks in 2023 to 11.1 weeks in 2026, and average duration from 20.4 to 25.1 weeks.

The report frames the problem as a hiring slowdown rather than a layoff wave. From 2023 to 2026 the hiring rate fell from 3.8% to 3.3%, quits from 2.4% to 2.0%, job openings from 5.8% to 4.4%, while layoffs held at 1.1%, below pre-pandemic levels. Hiring and quits both hit their lowest rates in the 11-year study period. The release cautions that the data show correlation, not causation.

Labor force participation among prime-age adults (25 to 54) reached 83.7%, the highest in the study, indicating workers are still engaged. Unemployment rose across groups versus 2019: ages 25 to 34 at 4.7% (from 3.8%), ages 25 to 54 at 3.7% (from 3.1%), ages 20 to 24 at 7.1% (from 6.9%), and bachelor's degree or higher age 25+ at 2.8% (from 2.2%). Adults 25 to 34 saw the largest increase.

Dr. Jasmine Escalera, Career Expert at MyPerfectResume, notes low layoffs make the market look stable but mask long searches. Boilerplate describes the resume builder, used by over 11 million job seekers since 2012.

claims.claim: More than one in four unemployed Americans are long-term unemployed (27+ weeks) in the first seven months of 2026, up from 2023.
The long-term unemployed population grew 68% since 2023.
Nearly 2 million Americans had been unemployed at least 27 weeks in May 2026.
The hiring rate fell to its lowest level in the 11 years studied.
Quits rate declined to the lowest in the period studied.
Layoffs rate remained flat and below pre-pandemic levels.
Job openings rate declined from 2023 to 2026.
Prime-age labor force participation reached the highest level in the study.
Unemployment among ages 25-34 rose compared with 2019, the largest increase among age groups studied.
Unemployment among those with a bachelor's degree or higher, age 25+, rose versus 2019.
Low layoffs mask the difficulty faced by people already out of work.
